title: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”: THE BIBLE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE A MAN UNTOUCHABLE
paragraphs: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”: THE BIBLE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE A MAN UNTOUCHABLE

What Psalm 105:15 really means—and why the same Bible that commands honor never commands you to surrender discernment, excuse sin, silence truth, or give any human being the place that belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
There are Bible verses people run to when they are afraid.
There are Bible verses people cling to when they are hurting.
And then there are Bible verses people sometimes use to make other people afraid.
“Touch not mine anointed.”
Five words from the King James Bible.
Five words that have comforted believers.
Five words that have also been whispered from pulpits, thrown across arguments, posted beneath accusations, and used as a spiritual warning:
Be careful what you say about me.
Don't question the pastor.
Don't challenge the prophet.
Don't expose the leader.
Don't criticize the man of God.
Touch not God's anointed.
And suddenly, a frightened believer begins wondering whether asking an honest question might put them in rebellion against God.
Maybe you have been there.
Maybe something didn't look right, but you were afraid to say it.
Maybe someone with a title wounded you, manipulated you, embarrassed you, or behaved in a way that contradicted Scripture—and when questions began rising inside you, another voice rose even louder:
Don't touch God's anointed.
So you stayed quiet.
But what if the verse is being asked to carry a meaning its original context never gave it?
What if honoring God's servants and testing what they teach are not enemies?
What if biblical submission never required spiritual blindness?
And what if the most dangerous thing about misusing “Touch not My anointed” is that it can slowly move our eyes away from the One Anointed King whom Scripture ultimately calls us to worship?
Before you defend the phrase…
before you reject it…
before you use it against somebody…
open the Bible.
Because context changes everything.

Psalm 105 remembers God's covenant faithfulness to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants. The psalmist describes a vulnerable people—few in number, strangers moving from nation to nation—whom God sovereignly protected. Psalm 105:14 says that God permitted no one to oppress them and even rebuked kings for their sake. Then comes the famous declaration:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”

That same wording appears in 1 Chronicles 16:22 in David's song of thanksgiving. The surrounding passage likewise remembers God's covenant and His protection of His people before calling the earth to proclaim His salvation and glory.
Now look closer.
The Hebrew of Psalm 105:15 reads:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וְלִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
’Al-tigge‘u vimshichai, velinvi’ai ’al-tare‘u.
The important expression is בִמְשִׁיחָי — bimshichai, commonly rendered “My anointed ones.”
Notice something that can disappear when people quote the familiar English phrase casually:
It is plural.
“My anointed ones.”

The Hebrew mashiach is associated with someone anointed or set apart, and the form in Psalm 105:15 refers to God's “anointed ones.” The accompanying phrase speaks of “My prophets.” The verb translated “touch” comes from naga‘, a word that can mean to touch, reach, or strike, while the final expression forbids doing evil or harm to God's prophets.
That matters enormously.
Psalm 105 is not originally presenting a modern pastor standing behind a pulpit and declaring himself immune from examination.
Read backward.
The psalm remembers Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
The covenant.
A small wandering people living among nations more powerful than themselves.
“They went from one nation to another,” the psalm recalls, while God protected them and rebuked kings on their behalf. Then comes the declaration not to touch His anointed ones or harm His prophets.
The picture is not primarily an influential religious leader protecting his reputation from criticism.
It is the powerful God protecting vulnerable covenant people.
That turns the emotional direction of the verse almost completely around.
The text so often used by powerful people to warn vulnerable people was originally spoken in the context of God defending vulnerable people from powerful people.
Read that again.
God is the Protector in Psalm 105.
His covenant faithfulness is the story.
His sovereignty is the security.
His glory is the point.

That doesn't mean Christians should become disrespectful toward pastors, elders, teachers, or other believers. Scripture repeatedly calls Christians toward honor, love, humility, peace, and proper respect for faithful spiritual leadership.
Nor does this mean slander suddenly becomes acceptable.
It doesn't.
False accusations are still sinful.
Gossip is still destructive.
Maliciously trying to ruin someone is not Christian discernment.
Celebrating another person's downfall is not holiness.
You can be correct about someone's failure and still be sinful in the way you talk about it.
But there is a canyon between slander and biblical discernment.
There is a difference between attacking someone and testing someone's teaching.
There is a difference between rebellion and refusing to participate in wrongdoing.
There is a difference between dishonoring faithful leadership and holding leadership accountable to the Word of God.
And Scripture itself proves it.
Think about David and Saul.

David famously refused to kill Saul because Saul was “the LORD's anointed.” When David had opportunities to take Saul's life, he would not stretch out his hand to destroy the king. That demonstrates a profound fear of God and refusal to seize vengeance for himself.
But notice what David did not do.
He did not pretend Saul was behaving righteously.
He did not call Saul's murderous pursuit holy because Saul had been anointed.
He did not conclude that anointing transformed evil behavior into good behavior.
He could respect the office, refuse personal vengeance, entrust judgment to God—and still recognize that Saul was trying to kill him.
Biblical honor did not require biblical amnesia.
And that distinction could set somebody free.
You do not need to hate someone to tell the truth.
You do not need to destroy someone to establish boundaries.
You do not need to become bitter to recognize wrongdoing.
You do not need to appoint yourself judge, jury, and executioner.
And you certainly do not need to pretend darkness is light because the person responsible carries a Bible.
Jesus never asked you to surrender truth in order to protect someone's religious image.
In fact, the New Testament repeatedly assumes that claims and teachings must be tested.
The Bereans were praised because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether what Paul preached was true (Acts 17:11).
Think about how extraordinary that is.
Paul was an apostle.
Yet Scripture does not rebuke the Bereans for checking his message against Scripture.
It commends them.
Paul himself later tells believers, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).
John warns Christians not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits (1 John 4:1).
Paul publicly confronted Peter when Peter's behavior compromised the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
And the pastoral qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 would make little sense if Christian leaders were never allowed to have their character examined.
Biblical authority therefore cannot mean:
Never question me.
It means authority itself remains underneath the authority of God.
Every pastor is underneath Christ.
Every teacher is underneath Christ.
Every prophet is underneath Christ.
Every ministry is underneath Christ.
Every church is underneath Christ.
Every Christian platform is underneath Christ.
Every person writing an article like this is underneath Christ.
Including us.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Examine the context.
Test what you read.
Search the Scriptures.
Because the goal of Christian ministry should never be to make people dependent upon the personality delivering the message.
The goal is to bring people nearer to Jesus.
And this is where the phrase becomes even more beautiful.
Because the Bible's language of “anointed” ultimately draws our attention toward the supreme Anointed One.
Jesus Christ.
The Greek word Χριστός — Christos, “Christ,” means the Anointed One and corresponds to the messianic concept expressed by Hebrew mashiach.
“Christ” is not Jesus' surname.
It is a royal, messianic declaration.
Jesus is the Christ.
The Anointed King.
The promised Messiah.
The One before whom every earthly title eventually becomes small.
And look at what happened to God's ultimate Anointed One.
He was touched.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Struck.
Falsely accused.
Scourged.
Nailed to a cross.
A crown of thorns was pressed onto His head.
Blood ran down His face.
People mocked His kingship while the true King stood before them.
The hands that had healed the sick were pierced.
The feet that carried good news were nailed down.
The voice that commanded storms was mocked by men whose lungs were being sustained by His power.
And He could have ended it.
Yet He stayed.
Not because evil had won.
Because redemption was being accomplished.
This is where “Touch not My anointed” collides with the scandal of the Gospel.
The Anointed One allowed wicked hands to seize Him so guilty people like us could be reconciled to God.
He bore sin.
He endured shame.
He died.
And then…
the grave discovered it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
Jesus rose.
That is Christianity.
Not celebrity Christianity.
Not personality Christianity.
Not untouchable-leader Christianity.
Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
And when you see Him clearly, something begins changing inside you.
You stop asking, “Which Christian personality am I supposed to defend at all costs?”
And you begin asking:
“Is Jesus being honored?”
“Is Scripture being handled faithfully?”
“Is sin being confronted with truth and grace?”
“Are wounded people being shepherded or silenced?”
“Is repentance expected from everyone—or only from people without titles?”
Because repentance has no VIP section.
The pastor needs grace.
The congregation needs grace.
The preacher needs forgiveness.
The listener needs forgiveness.
The famous Christian needs Jesus.
The anonymous Christian needs Jesus.
The person who wounded you needs Jesus.
And you need Jesus too.
That last part matters.
Because an article about abusive authority can easily become an excuse to examine everybody except ourselves.
We can become experts at identifying someone else's manipulation while remaining blind to our own pride.
We can expose hypocrisy while secretly feeding hatred.
We can demand another person's repentance while refusing to forgive.
We can correctly identify a leader's sin and then allow bitterness to become ours.
Jesus does not merely want to rescue you from someone else's darkness.
He wants to rescue you from yours.
Maybe your wound is real.
Maybe the betrayal happened.
Maybe the spiritual intimidation was devastating.
Maybe someone used God's name to control you.
If so, calling evil “evil” is not the same thing as abandoning Christ.
But do not allow what a flawed Christian did to you to convince you that Jesus is like them.
People can misuse His name.
They cannot change His character.
A shepherd may fail you.
The Good Shepherd remains good.
A father may abandon you.
Your heavenly Father has not changed.
A Christian may lie to you.
Jesus remains the Truth.
A church may wound you.
Christ still bears scars Himself.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needed tonight:
Do not confuse the person who wounded you in Jesus' name with Jesus Himself.
Come back to Christ.
Not necessarily back to an unsafe situation.
Not back to manipulation.
Not back to pretending.
Back to Christ.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the memories you keep replaying at 2:13 in the morning.
Bring Him the church hurt you don't know how to explain without crying.
Bring Him your cynicism.
Bring Him your shame.
And bring Him your own sin too.
Because the Gospel is not merely God exposing bad leaders.
The Gospel is God rescuing sinners.
All kinds of sinners.
People in pews.
People behind pulpits.
People holding microphones.
People hiding behind screens.
You.
Me.
All of us stand in desperate need of the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
That is why accountability should never thrill us because someone is falling.
It should break our hearts because sin destroys.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become permission.
Jesus gives us neither counterfeit.
He is full of grace and truth.
So honor faithful leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Protect them from malicious lies.
Do not participate in gossip disguised as discernment.
Do not treat pastors as disposable simply because they are imperfect human beings.
But never turn honor into idolatry.
Never give a spiritual leader the authority to rewrite Scripture.
Never allow charisma to outrank character.
Never let someone's “anointing” become an excuse for unrepentant sin.
And never surrender the throne of your conscience to a human being.
That throne belongs to God.
If you are a Christian leader reading this, there is something here for you too.
The safest response to criticism is not always:
“Touch not God's anointed.”
Sometimes the holiest response is:
“Lord, search me.”
Maybe the accusation is false.
Then walk faithfully and trust God with your name.
But maybe part of it is true.
Maybe somebody saw what you refused to see.
Maybe success made correction increasingly difficult.
Maybe the ministry became so important that protecting the organization began feeling more urgent than protecting people.
Maybe “God told me” started ending conversations Scripture should have been allowed to examine.
If conviction is knocking, don't barricade the door with Psalm 105:15.
Open it.
Repentance is not the destruction of a ministry.
Sometimes repentance is the first evidence that the ministry still belongs to Jesus.
Peter failed terribly.
Jesus restored him.
David sinned grievously.
When confronted, he confessed.
The Gospel does not require flawless servants.
It produces repentant ones.
There is no shame in falling before Christ and saying:
“I was wrong.”
There is danger in becoming too important to say it.

Maybe this article exposed something you have carried silently for years. If it did, you don't have to tell strangers every detail of your pain. But you also don't have to keep pretending nothing happened.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person struggling.
That matters.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who quietly reads your posts to follow too.
We will not put words in God's mouth.
But hear this clearly:
It doesn't.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support ministry because you freely want the Gospel proclaimed, believers strengthened, biblical resources created, and more wounded and wandering people pointed toward Christ.
Give freely.
Share freely.
Serve freely.
And glorify God above every ministry—including this one.
Because one day there will be no famous pastors.
No follower counts.
No verified badges.
No platforms.
No bestselling books.
No impressive ministry statistics.
No Christian celebrities.
There will be a King.
And every one of us will stand before Him.
So perhaps the question was never merely:
“Who is God's anointed?”
Perhaps the question beneath the question is:
What have you done with God's Anointed One?
Jesus Christ.
Have you admired Him without surrendering?
Quoted Him without obeying?
Defended Christianity without actually knowing Christ?
Protected religious appearances while hiding sin?
Then stop hiding.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
The cross is proof that your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe—and God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
You don't need an untouchable preacher.
You need an unstoppable Savior.
You don't need a religious celebrity who can never be questioned.
You need the Christ who already knows every question, every wound, every secret, every failure—and still calls sinners to come, repent, believe, and be made new.
And maybe that is why this verse needed to be rescued from the slogan it became.
Because Psalm 105:15 was never permission to make a human being untouchable.
It was a testimony that God's covenant people were never beyond His protection.
And the Gospel takes us further still.
Our ultimate hope is not that nobody will ever touch us.
Our hope is that even when this broken world wounds us, nothing can tear Christ's redeemed people from the hands of their Savior.
So test everything.
Reject slander.
Honor what is honorable.
Expose darkness truthfully and responsibly.
Forgive without calling evil good.
Seek justice without worshiping vengeance.
Repent when you are wrong.
Protect the vulnerable.
Pray for faithful shepherds.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because pastors do not rewrite everything.
Prophets do not rewrite everything.
Churches do not rewrite everything.
Influencers do not rewrite everything.
Jesus does.

And when human hands have written shame across your story, when spiritual wounds have written distrust across your heart, when your own sins have written chapters you desperately wish you could erase…
remember this:
The hands they pierced are still the hands capable of rewriting your story.
